A Deal With Mediators and No Second Party

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reportedly agreed overnight to a compromise drafted by Qatari and US mediators for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, according to two diplomats cited by Israel's Channel 12. 

His approval was framed as one of the reasons Trump called off the weekend strike, 

The technical detail sells it: ships enter the Gulf through Iranian waters, and exit through Omani waters. That's oddly specific for something that might not exist.

Oman signed off too, but with a catch. Muscat wants confirmation that Araghchi's yes actually speaks for the Revolutionary Guards, not just the foreign ministry, and Qatari mediators are still working the phones to secure that buy-in. 

In other words, the deal celebrated in Washington is still waiting on approval from the people who actually hold the keys to the strait. Al Jazeera's Mehjoob Zweiri, director of the Gulf studies center at Qatar University, added the more cautious framing: "Iran received a proposal from the United States that could lead to a reduction in current tensions, and Tehran is studying it seriously." Studying. Not signing.

And then Tehran's own state media pulled the rug out entirely. Iran's semi-official Fars News quoted a member of the negotiating team calling the Israeli media report "false," with a military source insisting the strait stays closed to any vessel that doesn't coordinate with the Revolutionary Guards. 

So within hours of Trump citing this agreement as his reason for standing down, Iran's own press denied the agreement exists.

A deal that has mediators, diplomats, and a press release, but apparently no confirmed signature from either government involved. Trump built a strike cancellation on top of it anyway. 

What exactly did Washington agree to stop bombing over?

📡 Industry minister travels to Pakistan for trade, free trade talks

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Minister of Industry, Mine and Trade, Mohammad Atabak, has traveled to Islamabad, leading a high-level delegation of government officials and private sector representatives for talks aimed at expanding economic, trade and industrial cooperation.

Starting on Monday, the two-day official visit includes participation in the 10th meeting of the Iran–Pakistan Joint Trade Committee and a meeting with Pakistan’s prime minister.
​
The agenda covers 19 key issues, including finalizing the text of a free trade agreement between the two neighboring countries, establishing a barter mechanism, and reviewing bilateral trade agreements.
​
The two sides are also expected to discuss easing transit barriers and facilitating the movement of Iranian containers through Pakistani ports.
​
The talks will address plans to develop border infrastructure at the Gabd–Rimdan crossing, create a new road to the Pakistani border, and improve cross-border road transport.
​
The discussions will also focus on maritime and rail connectivity, including linking the Gwadar maritime border with Rimdan and expanding the rail corridor between the ports of Chabahar and Gwadar.
​
Other issues include promoting joint industrial production, particularly in textiles, resolving banking and financial obstacles facing traders, facilitating business visas and activating joint border markets as part of efforts to advance a bilateral trade roadmap targeting $10 billion in annual trade.
